questions.prompt: When can Git perform a fast-forward merge?

options.text: When the current branch hasn't diverged, so the pointer just moves forward
Only when there is a conflict
When both branches changed the same lines

questions.explanation: If the target branch has no commits the other lacks, Git simply advances its pointer to the tip — a fast-forward, with no merge commit.

questions.prompt: How many parents does a merge commit have?

options.text: It depends on the number of files changed

questions.explanation: A merge commit records two (or more) parents — one for each branch being combined — which is what distinguishes it from an ordinary commit.

questions.prompt: Which statements about merge conflicts are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They occur when both branches change the same lines differently
You resolve them, then git add and commit
Git always resolves every conflict for you automatically

questions.explanation: Overlapping changes cause conflicts, Git brackets the competing versions with markers, and you finish by staging and committing. Git cannot decide overlapping changes for you.

questions.prompt: To cancel an in-progress merge and return to the previous state, run: git merge --______
questions.explanation: git merge --abort restores the repository to exactly how it was before you started the merge.

questions.prompt: A three-way merge combines which three commits?

options.text: The first, middle, and last commits of the branch
The two branch tips and their common ancestor
The local, staged, and committed versions

questions.explanation: A three-way merge uses the two branch tips plus their common ancestor (the merge base) to work out how to combine the changes.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Pointer moves ahead; no merge commit
Merge commit from two tips + common ancestor

questions.explanation: Fast-forward avoids a merge commit, a three-way merge creates one, the markers bracket competing versions, and --abort backs out.
